hits.title: Show HN: Learnmap, learn programming in a playful way
hits.author: erikpau
hits.story_text:
Even while a large majority of people will program with an LLM these days, people are still learning programming languages, and the demand to "how to learn language X" is still strong.

Learnmap allows you to learn a language by picking your own path, with your own goal. 15+ languages are supports (Rust, Zig, Nim, Go, TS, and many more), and more are coming.

hits.title: Show HN: Jam – A music making game where you play gigs to earn studio gear
hits.author: garrinm
hits.story_text:
The idea comes from Chrome Music Lab, which was addictive and satisfying. I felt it could be that fun and easy to put down musical ideas and hear them grow into something more substantial. Simple at first, but with progressively more depth if the player wants to go there. That was the seed, and it spiraled from there into Jam.

You start with one instrument, and you write parts on a piano roll. Create your own music or play gigs (levels) to earn coins and buy more gear. Each gig is built around one musical idea, so you pick up some music knowledge as you go. Friends can join your studio with a link and write parts alongside you.

In my other Show HNs I've always come with my own code. In this case I didn't write the code, but I'm still proud of the outcome and I hope some of you will enjoy it too.

The audio code is Rust/WASM running in a worklet. This is the part I had prior experience in, and it's been fun getting that into a browser. The instruments are decent and the signal chains hold their own. The front end is the agent's own design in three.js. The optimization work there was interesting because of how busy the UI gets and how many elements come into view. I focused on measuring React renders per interaction, instruction counts for the audio engine, load times and frame times. The result is something that runs decently even on a phone.

The multiplayer side is simple. Each studio is a Cloudflare Durable Object that holds the song. Players connect to it over a WebSocket and send small actions (add a note, turn a knob). The object applies each action, stores the result and sends the updated session to anyone else in the room. This simple setup allows collaborative music making out of the gate, even though it's not the game's main focus (yet).

This is a beta: feedback, comments and criticisms are all welcome. You can get into the game with no signup, and if you want to save your progress you'll be prompted to enter an email address.

hits.title: Show HN: Straum – a Postgres materialized view that is never stale
hits.author: jeeybee
hits.story_text:
I've seen too many slow-log queries with a GROUP BY that makes Postgres blow up, so for the last two weeks or so I've been working on Straum. You declare the aggregates as a view, and Straum answers over HTTP (other transports might be added). I've been using the New York taxi dataset as a benchmark. On the heavier GROUP BYs I see about 1,000x to 5,000x. It's written in Rust (of course).

It leans on Postgres replication slots, logical or physical, to get its data. Postgres stays the source of truth.

Benchmark: https://janbjorge.github.io/straum/benchmark.html Repo: https://github.com/janbjorge/straum

hits.title: Show HN: I got Modern Combat 2 – Black Pegasus running in a browser
hits.author: aryanbaburajan
hits.story_text:
I got Modern Combat 2: Black Pegasus running in a browser, with mouse and keyboard controls and online multiplayer.

Under the hood, a Rust ARM emulator compiled to WebAssembly runs the original Android binary.

This game used to be my childhood, playing it with my brother on the Blackberry Playbook. But it no longer ran on modern Android versions, so I thought I would port it - and even have it playable on desktop!

You'll need to bring your own APK and data file because of copyright reasons. For footage, check out my original tweet instead: https://x.com/aryanbaburajan/status/2123574545990799534

hits.author: emschwartz
hits.story_text:
If you're working with coding agents on a Rust code base, how are you handling the agent development loop, building, linting, and testing?

Are you running lots of agents locally in different worktrees? Are you pushing tons of PRs and do you have a massive CI bill?

Do you run everything through Cargo, Bazel, Buck2, something else?
